title: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where each position holds the number of days you must wait until a warmer temperature. If no warmer day exists, put 0.
shortTitle: Daily Temperatures: decreasing stack of indices
keyPoints: Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices; when a warmer day arrives, pop each colder index and record the distance.
Store indices on the stack rather than values because the answer is the gap in days, not the warmer value itself.
Use strictly-greater comparison so equal temperatures do not falsely resolve each other.
Time is O(n) because each index is pushed once and popped at most once despite the inner while loop.
Indices left on the stack at the end have no warmer day ahead; the answer array defaults to zero for them.
This is the Next Greater Element pattern adapted to return distances instead of values.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push indices on a decreasing stack; when a warmer day comes, pop each colder index and record current minus popped as the wait.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Daily Temperatures** – a monotonic stack problem that computes, for each day, how many days until a strictly warmer temperature.
- **Index stack** – store indices rather than values because the answer is the distance in positions, not the warmer value.
- **Decreasing stack** – the stack holds indices whose temperatures decrease from bottom to top, so the top is always the coldest pending day.
- **Resolution** – when a warmer day arrives, pop each colder index and set `answer[poppedIndex] = currentIndex - poppedIndex`.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time and O(n) space; each index is pushed and popped at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya tracks a daily market sentiment score at National Bank of India and wants to know, for each day, how many days she waited until sentiment rose above that day's level. She keeps a pile of pending day numbers. When a higher-score day arrives, it resolves every pending day on top, and the answer is today minus that day. Days left on the pile at the end never saw a higher score, so their wait is zero.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Daily Temperatures is the Next Greater Element pattern adapted to return distances instead of values. I keep a monotonic decreasing stack of indices and scan the array once. When a warmer day arrives, it resolves every pending colder day on the stack, and the answer for each resolved day is the current index minus the popped index.

Storing indices rather than values is essential because the answer is the gap in days, not the warmer temperature itself. The stack maintains a decreasing order from bottom to top, so the top is always the coldest pending day. When a new temperature is strictly greater than the top, I pop and record the distance, then keep popping until the invariant is restored. The strictly-greater comparison prevents equal temperatures from falsely resolving each other.

The time complexity is O(n) despite the inner while loop, because each index is pushed once and popped at most once across the entire scan. Indices remaining on the stack at the end have no warmer day ahead, and the answer array defaults to zero, so no cleanup is needed.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I used this to compute a days-to-recovery metric for a daily market sentiment index. One linear pass over a long trading history produced the full answer array, and the monotonic stack gave the dashboard responsive analytics even on months of daily data.

Remember one sentence: push indices on a decreasing stack, pop and record the gap when a warmer day arrives, and each index is handled at most twice for O(n) total.
